mission: Produces a settlement-source map of every open Kalshi and Polymarket weather/event contract, a two-week side-by-side log of a Raspberry Pi sensor against the exact station each contract settles on, and a paper-only trading arm for the final six hours before resolution that tests both the sensor edge and the 99c limit-order harvest against a control. Done means a measured answer to one question: does your own read of the settlement variable arrive earlier or more accurately than the public feed the market already prices? No real money moves until the paper arm beats its control after fees.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A professional weather-derivatives trader would start from the contract rules, not the sensor: which station ID, which report (NWS Daily Climate Report, a Weather Underground history page, an ASOS METAR), what rounding and unit conversion, and what time window. They would then measure the latency chain of that exact source, from sensor sampling to METAR issuance to the climate report to the market price move, and only buy hardware if a gap exists in that chain. They would treat the 99c harvest as a short-volatility position and compute the tail: one wrong 99c fill erases about 99 winning ones.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: The rules text of each contract (Polymarket market description via the Gamma API at gamma-api.polymarket.com/markets, Kalshi market rules via the trade API v2 /markets endpoint and the contract terms). The settlement source itself: ASOS one-minute and five-minute data and raw METARs from the Iowa Environmental Mesonet ASOS archive and aviationweather.gov, including the T-group remark (temperature in tenths of a degree C) and the 6-hour max/min groups. NWS station observations from api.weather.gov/stations/{id}/observations. The order book history from the Polymarket CLOB API and websocket, and Kalshi orderbook snapshots. NASA EONET v3 events at eonet.gsfc.nasa.gov/api/v3/events for event contracts.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: Python with httpx and websockets for API pulls; pandas and parquet for logs; a BME280 or SHT45 on a Raspberry Pi over I2C inside a ventilated radiation shield at 1.5-2 m; chrony to keep the Pi clock within 50 ms; a latency ledger that timestamps when each source first shows a value. Evaluation: lead-lag cross-correlation between sensor, METAR and price; Brier score and log loss of your probability against the market-implied probability; Wasserstein distance (scipy.stats.wasserstein_distance) between the sensor-minus-station residual in week 1 and week 2 to catch drift; expected value per 99c fill net of fees with a bootstrap confidence interval.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: The settlement itself: the official value published by the source named in the rules, compared to your sensor's prediction of it, logged before the market resolved. A control arm that trades the same windows using only public METAR data, so any edge is attributable to the sensor. The venue's own resolution history for 99c contracts that resolved against the favorite, which gives the real tail frequency.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: You are a weather-derivatives analyst building a paper-only study. Do not place real orders. Step 1: pull every open weather and natural-event contract from the Polymarket Gamma API and the Kalshi trade API v2. For each, extract from the rules text: the settlement source (station ID, report name, URL), the variable (daily high, precipitation, event occurrence), unit and rounding rule, the observation window, and the resolution time. Output one parquet table and flag any contract whose rules are ambiguous. Step 2: for the three contracts whose station I can physically get near, build the latency chain: Iowa Environmental Mesonet ASOS one-minute data, METAR T-group and 6-hour max groups, the NWS Daily Climate Report, and the first order-book move. Record the timestamp each source first shows the final value. Step 3: specify a Raspberry Pi logger (SHT45 in a ventilated shield, chrony-synced clock) and a two-week comparison against the station feed. Step 4: define a paper arm for the final six hours before resolution with a control arm that uses public METAR only, max paper notional of 50 USD per contract and a 200 USD paper daily loss stop, plus a separate 99c harvest ledger with fees and tail losses. Step 5: report Brier score, lead time in minutes, and net expected value per trade with bootstrap intervals for both arms. State plainly if the sensor adds nothing over the public feed. Confirm venue legality for my jurisdiction before any step that touches an account.

one_shot:
ROLE AND STANCE
You are a quantitative analyst specializing in event and weather derivatives. Your job is to find out whether a cheap local sensor gives an earlier or more accurate read of a contract's settlement variable than the public data the market already prices. Source claims to test, not trust: a profile says a student made 100K+ USD on Polymarket weather contracts from a dorm weather station, and another says a trader harvests outcomes at 99c with 75 automated trades per hour.

CONTEXT
- Venues: Polymarket (Gamma API for market metadata, CLOB API and websocket for order books) and Kalshi (trade API v2, weather markets settling on NWS reports). Check legality for the user's jurisdiction first; Kalshi is US-regulated and Polymarket access varies.
- Settlement sources: ASOS stations, METAR reports (aviationweather.gov, Iowa Environmental Mesonet archive), NWS Daily Climate Report, api.weather.gov observations, Weather Underground station history pages where named in rules. Event contracts: NASA EONET v3 (no API key).
- Hardware: Raspberry Pi with an SHT45 or BME280 in a ventilated radiation shield, chrony time sync.
- Drift check from the source set: Wasserstein distance between backtest and live distributions.
- Insider-detection tools (Polymarket websocket forensics, QuiverQuant) are used ONLY to recognize price moves driven by information you lack. Never trade on non-public information about people.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
1. Paper only. No real order, no wallet signing, no API key with trade permission until the oracle gate below passes and the user explicitly approves.
2. Paper caps: 50 USD notional per contract, 200 USD paper loss per day stops the arm for that day, 1,000 USD total paper drawdown halts the study for review.
3. Every trading arm has a control arm trading the same windows on public METAR data only.
4. Fees and spread are charged on every paper fill at the venue's published rate.
5. Never promise or project returns. Report measured numbers with intervals.

DELIVERABLES IN ORDER
1. settlement_map.parquet: every open weather/event contract with station ID, report, variable, unit, rounding rule, window, resolution time, rules URL, and an ambiguity flag.
2. latency_chain.md: for the three chosen contracts, the timestamps at which sensor, ASOS one-minute, METAR T-group, 6-hour max group, climate report, and first order-book move each reflected the final value, over at least 10 resolved contracts.
3. sensor_spec.md and logger.py: wiring, siting, chrony config, one-minute CSV log, systemd unit.
4. paper_engine.py: final-six-hours watcher comparing sensor-implied probability to market-implied probability, with the control arm and the 99c harvest ledger, writing fills to paper_fills.parquet.
5. results.md: Brier score and log loss per arm, lead time distribution, net expected value per trade with bootstrap 95% intervals, 99c tail analysis (break-even win rate after fees and observed loss frequency), Wasserstein distance of the sensor residual week 1 vs week 2.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
Before finishing, write a GAPS section listing: contracts whose rules you could not parse; stations with no public one-minute data; any period where the Pi clock drifted more than 1 second; resolutions you could not match to an official value; any claim from the source posts you could not test. Fill every gap you can now (for example, pull the IEM archive instead of the live feed) and note what changed.

SELF-QUESTIONS (answer each in results.md)
- Does the rounding or C-to-F conversion of the settlement report change the winning bucket for readings near a boundary, and did I model it?
- Does the public METAR T-group already give the market the same information my sensor does, and how many minutes earlier?
- How many 99c fills would one loss erase after fees, and how often did 99c favorites lose in the venue's resolution history?
- Is the falsifier triggered: does the public intra-hour feed move price as fast as my sensor?

STOP CONDITIONS
Stop and report if: venue access is not legal for the user; fewer than 10 contracts resolve during the study; the paper drawdown cap trips; or the sensor leads the public feed by under 5 minutes on median, which means no exploitable latency edge.

ORACLE GATE FOR ANY REAL MONEY
Real money is only discussable if, over at least 30 resolved paper contracts, the sensor arm beats the control arm on Brier score and on net expected value with the bootstrap 95% interval excluding zero.

RETURN FORMAT
A short summary (verdict on sensor edge, verdict on 99c harvest, falsifier status), the file list above with paths, the GAPS section, and the self-question answers.

steps.title: Ground truth: settlement-source map
steps.goal: Know exactly which number, from which station and report, each open contract settles on.
steps.prompt: Pull every open weather and natural-event contract from the Polymarket Gamma API (gamma-api.polymarket.com/markets, filter by tag or keyword: temperature, rain, snow, hurricane, earthquake, wildfire) and from the Kalshi trade API v2 /markets endpoint (weather series such as daily high temperature by city). For each contract, read the full rules text and extract into settlement_map.parquet: venue, market ID, question, settlement source name, station ID (ICAO such as KNYC or KLGA where given), report type (NWS Daily Climate Report, METAR, Weather Underground history page, NASA EONET, other), variable, unit, rounding rule, observation window with timezone, resolution time, rules URL, and ambiguous (bool) with a one-line reason. Do not infer a station from the city name; if the rules do not name one, mark it ambiguous. Count contracts per settlement source. Before any of this, write one paragraph on whether the user's jurisdiction permits access to each venue and stop if it does not.
steps.expect: A parquet table with one row per open contract (typically dozens to a few hundred), every column filled or flagged, plus a count table by settlement source and a legality paragraph.
steps.audit: Pick 10 random rows and re-read the rules text by hand: station ID, rounding and window must match exactly. Any mismatch is a fail: fix the extractor and re-run on all rows. Fail also if more than 20% of rows are ambiguous without a reason.

steps.title: Latency chain of the public sources
steps.goal: Measure when each public source first reveals the settlement value, before buying any hardware.
steps.prompt: From settlement_map.parquet choose the three liquid contract series whose station you could get physically near. For each, pull 30 days of history: ASOS one-minute data from the Iowa Environmental Mesonet archive, raw METARs including the remarks T-group (temperature in tenths C) and 6-hour max/min groups, api.weather.gov observations, and the NWS Daily Climate Report issue time. Pull the matching order-book or trade history from the Polymarket CLOB API or Kalshi. For each resolved contract day, build a latency ledger: the timestamp when each source first showed a value that locked the final outcome bucket, and the timestamp when the market's best bid for the winning side first crossed 90c. Compute, per source, the median and 90th-percentile lead over that price move. Model the conversion and rounding the rules specify and flag days where conversion alone changed the bucket.
steps.expect: latency_chain.md with a table per series: source, median lead in minutes, p90 lead, plus a list of rounding-sensitive days and the raw ledger in parquet.
steps.audit: Recompute one day by hand from raw METAR text and confirm the ledger timestamp. If the market moves before every public source, assume a source you have not found and search the rules again before continuing.

steps.title: Build and site the sensor logger
steps.goal: Log a sensor reading comparable to the station's at one-minute cadence with a trustworthy clock.
steps.prompt: Write sensor_spec.md and logger.py for a Raspberry Pi with an SHT45 (or BME280) on I2C. Specify a ventilated radiation shield at 1.5 to 2 m, away from walls and pavement, mirroring ASOS siting as far as possible. Configure chrony against public NTP servers and log the clock offset each minute. logger.py reads the sensor every 10 s, writes one-minute mean, min, max and clock offset to a daily CSV, and pulls the station's latest observation from api.weather.gov alongside it. Ship a systemd service and timer, log rotation, and a health check that writes a heartbeat file. Then run for 14 days and produce residual.parquet: sensor minus station per minute, with hour-of-day and cloud cover from METAR. Note in sensor_spec.md the parts cost, power draw, and how to reproduce the install on a second Pi.
steps.expect: Wiring diagram in text, logger.py, chrony.conf snippet, systemd unit, and after 14 days a residual table with mean, standard deviation and hour-of-day bias.
steps.audit: Fail if clock offset ever exceeds 1 s, if more than 2% of minutes are missing, or if the residual standard deviation exceeds 1.5 C, which means siting is wrong; move the sensor and restart the 14 days.

steps.title: Sensor-implied probability model
steps.goal: Turn live sensor plus public data into a calibrated probability for each outcome bucket.
steps.prompt: Using residual.parquet and the latency ledger, build a model that, at any minute in the final six hours, outputs the probability of each settlement bucket. Inputs: current sensor reading corrected by the hour-of-day residual, running daily max so far, latest METAR T-group, forecast high from the NWS point forecast, minutes to window close. Use an empirical distribution of remaining rise given time of day and current gap, fit on the first 10 days, tested on the rest. Build an identical model that drops the sensor input and uses public data only; this is the control. Report Brier score and log loss for both on the held-out days, plus reliability diagrams. Save both fitted models with their training-day list so step 5 can load them unchanged.
steps.expect: model.py, a held-out comparison table of sensor model versus public-only model, and reliability plots.
steps.audit: Fail if the sensor model is fit and evaluated on the same days, or if any feature uses data timestamped after the prediction minute. Check with a shift test: shuffle sensor timestamps by 60 minutes and confirm skill drops.

steps.title: Paper engine with control and 99c ledger
steps.goal: Paper-trade the final six hours on both arms and the 99c harvest under hard caps.
steps.prompt: Write paper_engine.py, scheduled every minute in the final six hours before each chosen contract resolves. It reads the order book over websocket, computes market-implied probability from the mid, and the sensor-arm and control-arm probabilities from model.py. A paper buy fires only when model probability minus ask exceeds fees plus 3 percentage points. Caps: 50 USD paper notional per contract, 200 USD paper daily loss stop, 1,000 USD total paper drawdown halts everything. Separately, log every outcome trading at 99c or above in the same window, simulate a resting limit buy at 99c with queue position assumed last, and record its paper result after resolution. Every fill pays the venue's published fee and the spread. Write to paper_fills.parquet. The code must contain no order-placing call; assert that no trading credential is loaded.
steps.expect: A running engine, a fills table with arm, contract, time, price, size, fee, outcome, P&L, and a daily summary.
steps.audit: Grep the code for any order-submission endpoint and fail if found. Replay one resolved day offline and confirm fills reproduce. Fail if a fill uses a price better than the best ask at that timestamp.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Decide whether the sensor and the 99c harvest have edge, with evidence.
steps.prompt: After at least 30 resolved paper contracts, compute for each arm: Brier score, log loss, number of trades, net P&L, net expected value per trade with a bootstrap 95% interval (10,000 resamples by contract day). Compare sensor arm to control arm. For the 99c ledger, compute break-even win rate after fees, observed loss count, and the expected value per fill with interval; pull the venue's history of 99c favorites that lost to estimate tail frequency beyond your sample. Compute the Wasserstein distance between week-1 and final-week sensor residuals and between paper-period and backtest-period price distributions. Answer the falsifier directly: does the public intra-hour feed move price as fast as the sensor? Write results.md with a GAPS section: every claim from the source posts and from your own steps, marked verified, unverified or false with the evidence file. State the real-money gate result in one line; never recommend live trading if the interval includes zero.
steps.expect: results.md with per-arm tables, falsifier verdict, gap list and gate line.
steps.audit: Have the numbers recomputed from paper_fills.parquet by a fresh script and compare to two decimal places. Fail if any arm lacks a control comparison or if results quote returns without intervals.

gap_audit_prompt: You are auditing a finished paper study of sensor-settled prediction-market contracts. Open settlement_map.parquet, latency_chain.md, residual.parquet, paper_fills.parquet and results.md. List every factual claim in results.md, one per line. For each, mark verified (cite the file and row or computation that proves it), unverified (say what data would prove it), or false. Specifically check: that each traded contract's station and rounding rule match the rules text; that no feature in the model uses data after the prediction minute; that fees and spread were charged on every fill; that the control arm traded the same windows; that the 99c tail estimate uses more than your own sample; that the Pi clock stayed within 1 s; and that the source claims (100K+ USD from a dorm station, 75 trades per hour at 99c) are labeled unverified anecdotes, not evidence. Then list missing pieces: contracts never resolved, stations without one-minute data, days with logger outages. Rank problems by verdict impact. Fix the top three now by re-running the relevant computation, and report the before and after numbers. End with what you could not fix and why, and restate the real-money gate result.
self_questions: Which exact report and station does each contract settle on, and did I read it from the rules or guess it from the city?
Does C-to-F conversion or whole-degree rounding in the settlement report flip buckets near a boundary, and did my model include it?
Is my sensor measuring the station's air or my rooftop's, and how big is the hour-of-day bias?
Does the METAR T-group or 6-hour max group already reveal the final high before my sensor gives any extra information?
How many 99c wins does one 99c loss erase after fees, and how often do 99c favorites lose in venue history?
Could a price move I attribute to my edge be someone else's information that I should not be trading against?
Is the venue legal for this user, and did I keep every trading credential out of the code?
Did my sensor residual drift between week 1 and week 2, as measured by Wasserstein distance?
validation_oracles: The official settlement value published by the source named in the rules (for example the NWS Daily Climate Report) versus my logged pre-resolution prediction for every traded contract.
The public-METAR-only control arm trading identical windows: the sensor arm must beat it on Brier score and net expected value with a bootstrap 95% interval excluding zero over 30 or more contracts.
The venue's own resolution history for outcomes priced at 99c or above, giving the observed frequency of favorites losing.
A second person re-running latency_chain from the raw IEM and order-book files and reproducing median lead times within 1 minute.
failure_modes: Wrong station: the contract settles on Central Park but the sensor is compared to LaGuardia. Tell: residual looks fine but predictions miss the settled value. Fix: re-extract the station from rules text and re-run step 2.
Microclimate bias: rooftop sensor reads 2 C hot in afternoon sun. Tell: residual mean depends strongly on hour and cloud cover. Fix: ventilated shield, re-site, hour-of-day correction.

No latency edge: the market reaches 95c from the METAR T-group before the sensor adds anything. Tell: median sensor lead under 5 minutes. Fix: accept the falsifier and stop; do not tune until it looks good.

99c tail blindness: weeks of 1c wins then one loss erases them. Tell: zero losses in sample but break-even win rate above 99%. Fix: use venue-wide history for tail frequency and report expected value with that rate.
Fantasy fills: paper engine fills at mid or at prices not on the book. Tell: sensor arm P&L far above what visible depth allows. Fix: fill at best ask, size capped by displayed depth.
agent_direction: Start with the APIs, not hardware: Polymarket Gamma and CLOB, Kalshi trade API v2, Iowa Environmental Mesonet ASOS archive, api.weather.gov. Cache every raw response to data/raw/ as dated JSON or parquet so steps can be re-run offline. Spawn one sub-agent per venue for step 1 extraction and a separate one for the latency ledger in step 2; review their tables by re-reading 10 rules texts yourself. Stop and ask the user before anything involving accounts, credentials, or jurisdiction questions you cannot resolve from public venue terms, and before buying hardware if step 2 already shows no latency gap. Never load a key with trade permission; the engine must fail closed if one is present. Long waits are scheduled jobs: write the timers, return, resume from logs. Return files: settlement_map.parquet, latency_chain.md, sensor_spec.md, logger.py, model.py, paper_engine.py, paper_fills.parquet, results.md, all under one study folder, with results.md as the entry point.

mission: Produces a walk-forward study that runs the open Kronos candlestick foundation model zero-shot on two years of hourly BTC and QQQ, scores every forecast against naive baselines, and tests whether tradeability measures (Kaufman efficiency ratio, Lempel-Ziv complexity, Hurst exponent, Hidden Markov regime) sort Kronos's error. If they do, it fits a logistic tradeability gate and paper-trades Kronos only inside the gate against an ungated arm and a random gate of equal coverage. Done means a falsifier verdict with confidence intervals; no real money until the gated paper arm beats both controls after costs.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A quant researcher would never compare Kronos to nothing: they would score it against a random walk (last close) and an AR(1) on log returns, because the source survey itself says generic foundation models barely beat simple autoregressive baselines on stocks. They would compute every gate feature strictly from data available at the forecast time, use purged walk-forward splits, and test monotonicity of error across quintiles with a statistic, not a chart. They would include a random gate with the same coverage, since any filter that skips 40% of bars changes turnover and costs. They would also replicate the telonic claim that low-efficiency days made only about a third of the money before trusting the gate.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: The Kronos repo (github.com/shiyu-coder/Kronos) and its paper, the model weights on Hugging Face (NeoQuasar/Kronos-small, Kronos-base, and Kronos-Tokenizer-base), and the repo's prediction examples. Raw price data: Binance public kline archives at data.binance.vision for BTCUSDT 1h, and hourly QQQ bars from a broker or vendor history (yfinance caps hourly history near 730 days, so record the exact source and gaps). Perry Kaufman's efficiency ratio definition, the Lempel-Ziv 1976 complexity paper, and Hurst's rescaled range method as originally specified.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: Python, PyTorch, the repo's KronosPredictor with a 512-bar context window; pandas and parquet; antropy (lziv_complexity on binarized returns); nolds (hurst_rs, dfa, lyap_r); hmmlearn GaussianHMM with 3 states fit only on past data; scikit-learn LogisticRegression with the 15 lagged price features described by the telonic post; statsmodels for AR(1). Evaluation: MAE and RMSE of next-bar log return, directional hit rate, Diebold-Mariano test against the random walk, Spearman correlation of quintile rank to mean error, block bootstrap (stationary bootstrap, 24-bar blocks) for intervals, and a cost model of 5 bps per side for BTC and 1 bp plus spread for QQQ.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: The random-walk and AR(1) baselines on identical bars; a random gate with identical coverage; the out-of-sample final six months held back untouched until the method is frozen; the Kronos paper's reported metrics reproduced on its own example data before trusting your pipeline; and a second run with a different seed and context length giving the same quintile ordering.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: Act as a quant researcher. Paper only, no real orders. Clone github.com/shiyu-coder/Kronos, load NeoQuasar/Kronos-small and Kronos-Tokenizer-base, and first reproduce one of the repo's example forecasts to confirm the pipeline. Download BTCUSDT 1h from data.binance.vision and hourly QQQ for the same two years; log source and missing bars. Run Kronos zero-shot walk-forward with a 512-bar context, predicting one bar ahead, and log forecast, realized return and error for every bar. Run a random-walk and an AR(1) baseline on the same bars. For each bar, compute from past data only: 20-bar Kaufman efficiency ratio, Lempel-Ziv complexity of the last 128 sign-binarized returns, Hurst exponent by rescaled range over 256 bars, and a 3-state Gaussian HMM regime fit on trailing data. Bucket bars into quintiles per measure and report Kronos error minus random-walk error per quintile with block-bootstrap 95% intervals and a Spearman monotonicity test. If any measure sorts error, fit a logistic regression predicting next-period efficiency ratio above median, freeze it, and paper-trade Kronos direction only in the top predicted bucket against an ungated arm and a random gate of equal coverage, with 5 bps per side costs, 1% of paper equity per trade, and a 10% paper drawdown halt. Keep the last six months as untouched holdout. Report whether the falsifier fires: is Kronos error flat across tradeability quintiles?

one_shot:
ROLE AND STANCE
You are a quantitative researcher testing one hypothesis: tradeability measures predict where the Kronos foundation model has skill, so a gate can make a free model usable. The source posts are claims to test, not facts: one creator says a hedge-fund team stress test found Kronos 'failed on many levels'; another says a logistic regression forecasting next-day efficiency ratio improved almost every metric over two years out of sample and that predicted low-efficiency days produced about a third of the money; others assert low Lempel-Ziv complexity means more predictable, Hurst above 0.5 means trending, and HMMs beat lagging indicators.

CONTEXT
- Model: github.com/shiyu-coder/Kronos, weights NeoQuasar/Kronos-small and NeoQuasar/Kronos-Tokenizer-base on Hugging Face, KronosPredictor, 512-bar max context. It tokenizes OHLCV candles with binary spherical quantization and predicts autoregressively.
- Data: BTCUSDT 1h from data.binance.vision; QQQ hourly from the user's broker or vendor history. Two years each.
- Libraries: antropy, nolds, hmmlearn, scikit-learn, statsmodels, arch (for stationary bootstrap).

HARD CONSTRAINTS
1. Paper only. No broker connection with trade permission.
2. Every feature at bar t uses data up to and including t only. Every model (HMM, logistic gate) is refit walk-forward on trailing data.
3. The final six months are a holdout touched once, after all choices are frozen and written to frozen_config.json.
4. Every result is compared to a random walk, an AR(1), and, for the gate, a random gate of equal coverage.
5. Costs: 5 bps per side BTC, 1 bp plus half-spread QQQ. Paper sizing 1% of equity per trade, 10% paper drawdown halts the arm.
6. Never state or imply expected returns; report measured statistics with intervals.

DELIVERABLES IN ORDER
1. repro.md: one Kronos example from the repo reproduced, confirming the pipeline.
2. forecasts.parquet: every bar, Kronos forecast, baselines, realized return, errors.
3. features.parquet: efficiency ratio (20 bars), LZ complexity (128 binarized returns), Hurst R/S (256 bars), Lyapunov estimate (lyap_r, 512 bars, flagged as noisy), HMM state.
4. quintiles.md: per measure, per asset, Kronos error minus random-walk error by quintile, 95% block-bootstrap intervals, Spearman rho and p-value, directional hit rate per quintile.
5. gate.py and frozen_config.json: logistic regression on 15 lagged price features predicting next-period efficiency ratio above its trailing median; only built if quintiles.md shows a monotone relation.
6. paper.md: gated arm vs ungated arm vs random gate, net of costs, on the walk-forward period and then once on the holdout: hit rate, Sharpe with interval, max drawdown, turnover.
7. A replication of the telonic split: share of ungated P&L that came from predicted low-efficiency bars.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
Write a GAPS list before finishing: missing bars and how filled; any feature that could leak (for example HMM fit on the full series); measures whose estimates are unstable at this window length (Lyapunov usually is); which source claims you could not test (the hedge-fund stress test details are not public). Fill any gap you can now, such as refitting a leaking model walk-forward, and show the before and after numbers.

SELF-QUESTIONS
- Does Kronos beat the random walk at all before gating? If not, what is the gate gating?
- Is error lower in high-efficiency bars only because volatility is lower there? Did I normalize error by trailing volatility?
- Do the four measures agree, or does each pick different bars?
- Does the gate beat a random gate of equal coverage after costs, or is the improvement just fewer trades?
- Did any choice get made after looking at the holdout?

STOP CONDITIONS
Stop after quintiles.md if Kronos error minus random-walk error is flat across quintiles for every measure (Spearman p above 0.1 on both assets): the falsifier fires and the gate is decoration. Report that as the result.

ORACLE GATE
No real money unless, on the untouched holdout, the gated arm beats both the ungated arm and the random gate on net Sharpe with the bootstrap interval of the difference excluding zero. Even then, return the evidence to the user and stop.

RETURN FORMAT
Verdict (falsifier fired or not, per asset), the file list, the quintile table, the paper comparison table, GAPS, and answers to the self-questions.

steps.title: Ground truth: reproduce Kronos and pull raw data
steps.goal: Prove the Kronos pipeline matches the repo and assemble clean two-year hourly data.
steps.prompt: Clone github.com/shiyu-coder/Kronos, install its requirements, and load NeoQuasar/Kronos-Tokenizer-base and NeoQuasar/Kronos-small. Run the repo's prediction example unchanged and confirm your output matches the published example within plotting tolerance; write repro.md with commands, versions, device, and runtime per forecast. Then download BTCUSDT 1h klines for the last two years from data.binance.vision monthly archives and verify checksums. Pull QQQ hourly bars for the same period from the user's broker history or a vendor; if only yfinance is available, note the roughly 730-day cap and regular-hours-only bars. Write raw parquet files with a manifest listing source, row count, first and last timestamp, and every missing bar. Do not forward-fill prices silently; mark gaps. Also record GPU or CPU model, PyTorch version and Hugging Face revision hashes of both weights so later runs are reproducible.
steps.expect: repro.md, two raw parquet files, and a manifest with gap counts.
steps.audit: Fail if the example output differs materially from the repo's, if BTC has more than 0.5% missing hours, or if timestamps are not in one timezone. Fix before step 2.

steps.title: Walk-forward forecasts and baselines
steps.goal: Log a Kronos forecast and two baselines for every bar with no lookahead.
steps.prompt: For each asset, iterate bars from bar 513 onward. At bar t, feed Kronos the previous 512 OHLCV bars ending at t and predict bar t+1 close; record predicted log return, realized log return and absolute error. Use a fixed sampling setting (record temperature and sample count) and a fixed seed. On the same bars compute a random-walk forecast (zero return) and an AR(1) on log returns refit on the trailing 2,000 bars. Store all in forecasts.parquet. Report overall MAE, RMSE, directional hit rate and a Diebold-Mariano test of Kronos versus random walk per asset. Batch on GPU if available and checkpoint every 1,000 bars so the run can resume. Write a run log with start time, bars per minute and any skipped bars with reasons.
steps.expect: forecasts.parquet with roughly 17,000 BTC rows and fewer QQQ rows, plus an overall metrics table.
steps.audit: Spot-check 5 bars by recomputing the input window and confirming the last input bar is t, not t+1. Fail on any leak. If Kronos does not beat the random walk overall, note it; the study continues because the hypothesis is about conditional skill.

steps.title: Tradeability features from past data only
steps.goal: Compute each tradeability measure at every bar using trailing windows only.
steps.prompt: For each bar t compute: Kaufman efficiency ratio over 20 bars (absolute net change divided by the sum of absolute bar changes); Lempel-Ziv complexity via antropy.lziv_complexity on the last 128 returns binarized by sign, normalized; Hurst exponent with nolds.hurst_rs over 256 bars and DFA alpha with nolds.dfa as a cross-check; largest Lyapunov exponent with nolds.lyap_r over 512 bars, flagged as noisy; and a 3-state GaussianHMM on returns and absolute returns refit every 500 bars on trailing data only, recording the filtered state at t. Also compute trailing 24-bar realized volatility to normalize errors later. Write features.parquet and a summary of each feature's distribution and pairwise Spearman correlations. Also store each feature's window length and library version in a features_meta.json so step 6 can cite them exactly.
steps.expect: features.parquet aligned to forecasts.parquet, a correlation matrix, and distribution plots.
steps.audit: Recompute two bars' features by hand from raw closes. Fail if the HMM was ever fit on data after t. Check that Hurst values lie mostly between 0.3 and 0.8; if not, the window or method is wrong.

steps.title: Quintile test: does tradeability sort Kronos error?
steps.goal: Test the falsifier directly.
steps.prompt: Join forecasts and features. For each measure and asset, assign bars to quintiles using trailing quintile cut points (rolling 2,000 bars), not full-sample cuts. Per quintile report: Kronos MAE minus random-walk MAE, the same normalized by trailing volatility, directional hit rate, and bar count, with 95% stationary-bootstrap intervals using 24-bar blocks. Test monotonicity with Spearman correlation between quintile rank and mean excess error. Repeat with Kronos-base if compute allows and with context 256 to check robustness. Write quintiles.md with one table per measure and a plain verdict: does any measure sort Kronos skill on both assets? Plot excess error by quintile with interval bars for each measure and asset, and save the figures beside the tables. Keep the table format identical across measures.
steps.expect: quintiles.md with eight tables (four measures by two assets), intervals, rho and p-values, and a verdict line.
steps.audit: Fail if quintile cuts use future data or if the volatility-normalized result is missing; raw error falls in calm bars for every model, so only the excess over random walk counts. If flat everywhere, stop here and go to step 6 with the falsifier fired.

steps.title: Fit the gate and paper-trade three arms
steps.goal: Build the logistic gate only if step 4 passes and compare it to honest controls.
steps.prompt: Build 15 lagged price features at bar t (returns over 1, 3, 6, 12, 24 bars; efficiency ratio over 10, 20, 50; volatility ratios; range-to-close; distance from 50-bar mean; the step 3 measures). Target: next-period efficiency ratio above its trailing median. Fit scikit-learn LogisticRegression walk-forward, refit monthly on trailing data. Freeze all settings in frozen_config.json before looking at the final six months. Paper arms: ungated (trade Kronos direction every bar), gated (trade only when gate probability is in its top quintile), random gate (same coverage, random bars, 100 seeds). Costs 5 bps per side BTC, 1 bp plus half-spread QQQ; size 1% of paper equity; 10% paper drawdown halts an arm. Also replicate the telonic split: share of ungated P&L earned on predicted low-efficiency bars.
steps.expect: gate.py, frozen_config.json, paper.md with a three-arm table per asset, and the telonic replication number.
steps.audit: Confirm frozen_config.json timestamp precedes the holdout run. Fail if the gated arm is not compared to the 100-seed random-gate distribution, or if costs are missing from any arm.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Run the holdout once, state the verdict, and list what is unproven.
steps.prompt: Run the frozen pipeline once on the final six months. Report for each asset: Kronos versus random walk Diebold-Mariano, quintile excess-error table, and the three paper arms with net Sharpe, max drawdown and turnover, plus the bootstrap interval of gated-minus-ungated and gated-minus-random-gate Sharpe. State the falsifier verdict per asset. Then write a GAPS section: each source claim (Kronos fails a hedge-fund stress test; efficiency-ratio gating lifts nearly every metric; low LZ complexity means predictable; Hurst above 0.5 means trending; HMM beats lagging indicators) marked verified, unverified or false with the file and number that decides it. List leaks found and fixed, unstable measures, and data gaps. State the real-money gate result in one line. Attach the plots from step 4 and the paper equity curves for all three arms.
steps.expect: final_report.md with verdicts, tables, GAPS, and gate line.
steps.audit: Recompute the holdout Sharpe from the raw paper fills with a fresh script. Fail if the holdout was run more than once or if any claim is marked verified without a cited number.

gap_audit_prompt: You are an independent reviewer of a study claiming tradeability measures gate the Kronos model. Open forecasts.parquet, features.parquet, quintiles.md, paper.md, frozen_config.json and final_report.md. List every quantitative claim in the reports. For each, recompute it from the parquet files with your own code and mark verified, unverified or false. Check for leakage specifically: shift every feature forward by one bar and confirm results get worse, not better; confirm quintile cut points and HMM fits used trailing data; confirm the holdout run time is after the frozen config. Check that errors were compared as excess over the random walk and normalized by trailing volatility, since calm bars shrink every model's error. Check the gated arm was compared to a random gate of equal coverage over at least 100 seeds. Check costs were applied per side on every trade. List missing pieces such as untested assets or context lengths. Rank problems by whether they could flip the falsifier verdict, fix the top three now, and report before and after numbers. Close with what you could not fix and why, and restate whether the no-real-money gate passed.
self_questions: Does Kronos beat a zero-return random walk on these bars before any gating?
Is lower error in high-efficiency bars just lower volatility, and did I normalize by trailing volatility?
Did any feature, quintile cut or HMM fit use data after bar t?
Do efficiency ratio, LZ complexity, Hurst and HMM state select the same bars, or does each tell a different story?
Is the Lyapunov estimate stable at 512 bars, or should it be reported as noise?
Does the gated arm beat a random gate of identical coverage, or is the gain just lower turnover and costs?
Did I make any choice after seeing holdout numbers?
Does the telonic 'about a third of the money' split replicate on hourly BTC and QQQ, or only on their daily strategy?
Are QQQ hourly bars regular-hours only, and does the overnight gap break the 512-bar context?
Would the result survive Kronos-base and a 256-bar context?
validation_oracles: The Kronos repo's own example forecast, reproduced exactly before any new run.
Random-walk and AR(1) forecasts on identical bars, with a Diebold-Mariano test per asset.
A 100-seed random gate with the same coverage as the learned gate; the gated arm must exceed its 95th percentile Sharpe net of costs.
The untouched final six months, run once after frozen_config.json is written.
An independent recomputation of the quintile table from raw parquet by a fresh script or second agent, matching to three decimals.
failure_modes: Volatility masquerading as skill: error falls in high-efficiency quintiles for Kronos and random walk alike. Tell: raw MAE drops but excess over random walk is flat. Fix: report only volatility-normalized excess error.
Lookahead in features: HMM or quintile cuts fit on the full series. Tell: suspiciously clean monotone quintiles. Fix: trailing refits, and a one-bar shift test that must make results worse.
Gate equals fewer trades: Sharpe rises because costs fall. Tell: random gate of equal coverage does as well. Fix: judge only against the random gate distribution.
Kronos has no unconditional skill: there is nothing to gate. Tell: Diebold-Mariano versus random walk not significant in any quintile. Fix: report the falsifier and stop.
Holdout contamination: thresholds tuned after a peek. Tell: holdout run timestamp before config freeze, or multiple holdout runs. Fix: declare result void and pick a new untouched window.
QQQ data artifacts: yfinance hourly gaps and session boundaries distort LZ and Hurst. Tell: features jump at market open. Fix: compute on session-aware returns or use vendor data.
agent_direction: Reach first for the Kronos repo and data.binance.vision; reproduce the repo example before writing anything new. Cache raw data and every forecast as parquet with checkpointing, because the Kronos walk-forward is the expensive step: on CPU it can take many hours, so run it as a background job and continue feature work in parallel. Spawn one sub-agent for feature computation (step 3) while the forecast job runs, and review its output by hand-recomputing two bars. Do not spawn agents for the holdout; run it yourself once. Stop and ask the user if no GPU is available and estimated runtime exceeds 24 hours, if QQQ hourly history is unavailable beyond yfinance, or if step 4 fires the falsifier, since steps 5 and 6 then change shape. Never connect a broker. Return files in one study folder: repro.md, forecasts.parquet, features.parquet, quintiles.md, gate.py, frozen_config.json, paper.md, final_report.md, with final_report.md as the entry point.

mission: Produces an underwriting pipeline for buying one small cash-flowing app under 50K USD and rebuilding it with an agent stack: a scored listing table from Acquire.com and Flippa, verified financials, a repo-comprehension pack (Gitingest, DeepWiki, GitDiagram, GitMCP), a rebuild spec with an hour estimate, a compliance and performance gap list, and a 90-day post-close plan with churn tracking. Done means the buyer can say, with evidence, whether rebuild plus migration costs less than six months of verified profit. No money is wired until a paper underwriting of three deals and an independent verification of revenue both pass.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A search-fund operator or micro-PE buyer would verify revenue from the payment processor and bank, never from seller screenshots, and would look at cohort churn, customer concentration and platform dependency before reading a line of code. They would underwrite on seller's discretionary earnings with a multiple, model the downside where traffic or an app-store listing disappears, and structure the deal as an asset purchase with escrow, an IP assignment, a transition period and a non-compete. On the technical side they would write characterization tests of current behavior before rewriting anything and migrate with a strangler pattern. They would treat the Bending Spoons story as survivorship: Evernote and Vimeo had brands; a 30K USD app may have nothing but a search rank.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: Listing pages and data rooms on Acquire.com and Flippa; read-only Stripe, Paddle or App Store Connect access and bank statements for 24 months; Google Search Console and analytics access; the actual git repository with full history; dependency manifests and lockfiles; hosting bills; support inbox exports; the privacy policy and terms as published; app-store review history. For the playbook itself: Bending Spoons' public statements and S-1 or IPO filings if available, and the public SaaS drawdown data behind the 'Atlassian -63%, HubSpot -48%, Workday -47%' claim.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: Claude Code with a Fable-orchestrates-Opus loop: the expensive model writes specs and reviews, cheaper subagents implement in parallel git worktrees. Repo comprehension by URL swap: gitingest.com for a single prompt-ready dump, deepwiki.com for generated docs, gitdiagram.com for architecture, gitmcp.io for live agent queries. Code facts: scc or cloc for size, git log churn analysis, gitleaks or trufflehog for secrets, osv-scanner for vulnerable dependencies, scancode-toolkit for license audit. Behavior: Playwright characterization tests, PostHog to learn which flows customers actually use. Earned autonomy per task type from the agentic-OS post: autonomy after 20 passes at 95%, revoked below 90%, and every API call checks stop_reason because refusals return HTTP 200. Valuation: seller's discretionary earnings, a downside scenario, payback months.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: Processor and bank data reconciled to the listing's claimed revenue within 5%; a lawyer's review of the asset purchase agreement; an escrow service holding funds until transfer; post-close monthly churn from the processor compared to the pre-close cohort baseline; the characterization test suite passing on old and new code; and the actual rebuild hours logged against the estimate.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: Act as a micro-acquisition analyst and technical due-diligence lead. I want to buy one software app under 50K USD and rebuild it with coding agents, Bending Spoons style. Do not contact sellers or move money; produce analysis only. First, scrape current Acquire.com and Flippa listings under 50K USD (respect each site's terms; if scraping is disallowed, use exports or manual copy). For each, record asking price, claimed trailing-12-month revenue and profit, multiple, age, stack, traffic source, platform dependency and churn if stated, then score revenue stability, stack age and replaceable share of code. Shortlist three. For each, write the diligence request list: read-only Stripe or App Store Connect access, 24 months of bank statements, Search Console, repo access under NDA. Specify the repo-comprehension pass with Gitingest, DeepWiki, GitDiagram and GitMCP, plus scc, gitleaks, osv-scanner and scancode. Draft a rebuild spec covering only flows PostHog shows customers use, with an hour estimate and the compliance gap list: privacy policy disclosure of data, AI use and third parties, deletion of uploads, private storage buckets, easy cancellation, trial-end reminders. Compute payback: rebuild plus migration hours times my hourly cost against six months of verified profit. Flag any deal where that ratio exceeds 1 or where verified revenue differs from the listing by more than 10%.

one_shot:
ROLE AND STANCE
You are a micro-acquisition analyst and technical diligence lead for a solo buyer who wants to apply the Bending Spoons playbook at small scale: buy a stagnant cash-flowing app, rebuild only the flows customers use with coding agents, expand margin. Treat the source posts as hypotheses. Claims to test: Bending Spoons grew from 40K USD to an 18B USD IPO this way; public SaaS multiples roughly halved; AI makes rebuilding cheap; a cron-driven orchestrator/executor loop with earned autonomy can run unattended; vibe-coded apps carry ten legal traps (one creator quotes 2,500 to 8,000 USD per user for privacy-policy gaps) and five performance gaps.

CONTEXT
- Deal sources: Acquire.com, Flippa. Structure: asset purchase agreement, escrow, IP assignment, transition support, non-compete.
- Repo comprehension: swap github.com in a URL for gitingest.com, deepwiki.com, gitdiagram.com, or gitmcp.io; press '.' on GitHub for browser VS Code. Reverse Engineer Anything for understanding behavior of code the buyer will own.
- Build loop: Claude Code, the expensive model plans and reviews, Opus subagents implement in parallel worktrees, review-fix loop until approved; autonomy per task type after 20 passes at 95%, revoked under 90%; check stop_reason on every call; daily regression tests.
- Analytics: PostHog installed first post-close to find used flows.
- Performance checklist: gzip or brotli on API responses, batched DB writes, profile round-trip latency to find the single slow step, optimistic UI, cached rendering.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
1. Analysis only. Do not contact sellers, sign anything, or move money. Purchase decisions return to the user.
2. Revenue counts only when reconciled to processor and bank data within 5%; screenshots are not evidence.
3. Paper underwriting first: fully underwrite three shortlisted deals as if buying, without buying, and record your predicted payback for later comparison.
4. Caps: purchase price at most 50K USD and at most 3x verified seller's discretionary earnings; rebuild budget at most 6 months of verified profit.
5. Legal and tax points are flagged for a lawyer or accountant; never presented as advice.
6. Reverse engineering applies only to code and systems the buyer owns or has written permission to analyze.

DELIVERABLES IN ORDER
1. listings.parquet with score columns and a ranked shortlist of three with reasons.
2. diligence_requests.md per shortlisted deal.
3. tech_dd.md per deal: scc size, churn hotspots, secrets found, vulnerable dependencies, license conflicts, architecture diagram link, hosting cost, single points of failure.
4. rebuild_spec.md: flows to keep, flows to drop, target stack, characterization tests, migration plan (strangler pattern), hour estimate with a range.
5. compliance_perf_gaps.md: each of the ten legal traps and five performance gaps marked present, absent or unknown with evidence.
6. underwriting.xlsx or .csv: price, verified profit, multiple, rebuild hours times hourly cost, payback months, downside case with 30% revenue loss, falsifier check.
7. post_close_plan.md: 90 days, PostHog first, monthly churn tracking against the pre-close cohort baseline.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
End with GAPS: every number not reconciled to source data; listing claims you could not verify; repo areas the comprehension tools could not explain; legal items needing a professional. Fill what you can now, for example by recomputing multiples from verified numbers.

SELF-QUESTIONS
- Is this app's value in code, or in a search rank or store listing that could vanish?
- What share of revenue comes from the top five customers?
- Does the hour estimate include data migration, support load and app-store review delays?
- Would rebuild plus migration cost more than six months of verified profit?
- Which of the ten legal traps already applies to the seller's current app, making me liable on day one?

STOP CONDITIONS
Stop and report if no listing survives revenue verification, if every shortlisted deal fails the payback test, or if repo access is refused.

RETURN FORMAT
Ranked shortlist with one-line verdicts, the file list, the underwriting table, GAPS, and self-question answers.

steps.title: Ground truth: listings and verified financials
steps.goal: Build a scored deal table from primary listing data and define what counts as verified revenue.
steps.prompt: Collect every current software listing under 50K USD on Acquire.com and Flippa. Check each site's terms first; if automated scraping is not allowed, use their export, saved searches, or manual copy into a sheet. For each listing record: URL, asking price, claimed trailing-12-month revenue and profit, implied multiple, business age, tech stack, monetization (subscription, one-time, ads), traffic sources, platform dependency (App Store, Shopify app store, Chrome Web Store), stated churn, and seller reason. Score 1 to 5 on revenue stability, stack age (older stack means more rebuild leverage and more risk), share of code plausibly replaceable, and platform risk. Write listings.parquet and a shortlist of three with reasons. For each shortlisted deal, write diligence_requests.md asking for read-only processor access, 24 months of bank statements, Search Console and analytics, support volume, hosting bills, and repo access under NDA.
steps.expect: listings.parquet with all fields, a top-three shortlist, and three request lists.
steps.audit: Recompute every multiple from price and profit. Fail if any listing lacks a source URL or if shortlist reasons rely on unverified seller claims without flagging them.

steps.title: Repo comprehension and technical diligence
steps.goal: Understand each shortlisted codebase fast and find hidden liabilities.
steps.prompt: For each shortlisted repo (only after access is granted under NDA), run: gitingest to produce a single text dump; DeepWiki for generated documentation if the repo is public or mirrored privately; GitDiagram for an architecture diagram; GitMCP so the agent can query the repo live. Then run scc for size and language mix, git log --numstat for churn hotspots over the last 12 months, gitleaks for committed secrets, osv-scanner on lockfiles for vulnerable dependencies, and scancode-toolkit for license conflicts. Identify single points of failure: one maintainer, one payment integration, unmaintained SDKs, hard-coded credentials. Write tech_dd.md per deal with findings, severity, and the estimated fix hours. Finally, list the three files or modules an executor agent would need to read first to change any core flow, and note where DeepWiki's generated docs disagreed with the code.
steps.expect: Three tech_dd.md files with tool output summaries, a diagram link or image, and a severity-ranked findings list.
steps.audit: Confirm each finding cites the tool output line. Fail if secrets are copied into the report; report only the file and rule ID. If a tool failed to run, mark that area unknown, not clean.

steps.title: Rebuild spec scoped to used flows
steps.goal: Specify the smallest rebuild that keeps paying customers.
steps.prompt: Using tech_dd.md, the seller's analytics, and support tickets, list every user-facing flow and mark it core, secondary, or dead. If usage data is weak, specify installing PostHog first post-close and deciding after two weeks of events. Write rebuild_spec.md: flows to keep, flows to drop, target stack, data model and migration plan using a strangler pattern (route one flow at a time to new code), characterization tests in Playwright for every core flow written against the old app before any rewrite, and an hour estimate per flow as low, expected and high. Include the five performance fixes as explicit tasks: response compression, batched writes, latency profiling, optimistic UI, cached rendering. Structure the work for an orchestrator that writes specs and reviews, and executor subagents in parallel worktrees, with autonomy granted per task type after 20 passes at 95%.
steps.expect: rebuild_spec.md with a flow table, test list, migration sequence and hour estimates with ranges.
steps.audit: Fail if any core flow lacks a characterization test or if the estimate omits data migration, support and app-store review delays. Sum hours and compare to a naive estimate from scc line counts; explain gaps over 2x.

steps.title: Compliance and performance gap list
steps.goal: Find liabilities the buyer inherits on closing day.
steps.prompt: For each shortlisted app, check the ten legal traps from the source post: no privacy policy; policy not disclosing data collection; policy not disclosing AI use; policy not naming third-party processors; uploads promised deleted but still stored; public storage buckets; fake testimonials; hard-to-cancel subscriptions; trial auto-charges without reminder; chatbots without self-harm handling. Inspect the live site, the policy text, storage configuration (bucket ACLs), subscription flow, and deletion code paths. The per-user fine figures in the post are claims; replace them with the actual governing rules (GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, state automatic-renewal laws, FTC guidance on reviews and negative-option billing) and mark each for lawyer review. Then measure the five performance gaps on the live app: response compression headers, write batching in code, request waterfall timing, UI update behavior, cache headers. Write compliance_perf_gaps.md with present, absent, unknown, evidence and fix hours.
steps.expect: A 15-row table per deal with evidence links or code references.
steps.audit: Fail if any row is marked absent without evidence. Do not test bucket access by downloading user data; check configuration only.

steps.title: Paper underwriting of three deals
steps.goal: Decide on paper whether the AI rebuild discount is real at this size.
steps.prompt: For each shortlisted deal, build underwriting.csv: asking price, verified trailing-12-month profit (or 'unverified' and excluded), multiple on verified profit, rebuild hours from rebuild_spec.md times the buyer's hourly cost, compliance and performance fix hours, migration cost, and payback months. Run a downside case with revenue down 30% and churn at twice the baseline. Apply the falsifier: rebuild plus migration cost above six months of verified profit, or expected post-migration churn above 10%, fails the deal. Apply caps: price at most 50K USD and at most 3x verified seller's discretionary earnings. Record predictions (hours, churn, payback) in predictions.json with a timestamp so a later actual can be scored against them. Compare to a control: what the same capital earns in a treasury bill over the payback period.
steps.expect: underwriting.csv, predictions.json, and a one-paragraph verdict per deal.
steps.audit: Fail if any input is unverified but used as verified. Recompute payback with a fresh script. Check the downside case is actually computed, not described.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: State which deal, if any, passes, and what remains unproven.
steps.prompt: Assemble final_report.md. For each deal: verified versus claimed revenue difference, tech findings by severity, compliance liabilities, payback base and downside, falsifier result, and a buy, pass or need-more-data verdict for the user to decide on. Write post_close_plan.md for the best deal: day 1 PostHog and credential rotation, weeks 1 to 2 characterization tests, weeks 3 to 10 strangler rebuild of core flows with daily regression tests in CI, monthly churn from the processor against the pre-close cohort. Then a GAPS section listing every source claim (18B USD IPO from 40K USD; public SaaS down roughly half; AI cheapens rebuilds; earned autonomy works unattended; the legal fine figures) as verified, unverified or false with evidence, and every deal number that is still seller-reported. Recommend which professional must review what before any money moves.
steps.expect: final_report.md, post_close_plan.md and a GAPS list.
steps.audit: Fail if a buy verdict rests on any unverified number or if the report omits the lawyer and escrow requirement. Cross-check three numbers against underwriting.csv.

gap_audit_prompt: You are an independent reviewer of a micro-acquisition package. Open listings.parquet, tech_dd.md files, rebuild_spec.md, compliance_perf_gaps.md, underwriting.csv, predictions.json and final_report.md. List every number and claim that supports a buy or pass verdict. Mark each verified (cite processor export, bank statement, tool output or code line), unverified (name the document that would prove it), or false. Specifically check: revenue reconciled to processor and bank within 5%; multiple computed on verified profit; rebuild hours include migration, support and store review; every core flow has a characterization test; secrets were not pasted into reports; each legal row cites the governing rule rather than a social-media fine figure; the downside case was computed; the falsifier threshold of six months of profit was applied. List missing items such as unrequested documents, unscanned repos, or untested flows. Rank by how much each could change a buy verdict, fix the top three now by recomputing or requesting the missing document in the requests list, and report before and after. End with what cannot be fixed without the seller, a lawyer or an accountant, and confirm no money moves before those reviews.
self_questions: Is the value in the code, or in a search rank, app-store listing or domain that a rebuild could lose?
Did I reconcile revenue to the processor and bank, or to the seller's dashboard?
What share of revenue sits with the top five customers, and what happens if one leaves at handover?
Does the rebuild estimate cover data migration, support load during cutover, and store review delays?
Which legal traps already exist in the seller's app and transfer to me at close?
Which flows does PostHog or the seller's analytics show customers actually use, versus what the code contains?
Is the stack old enough that rebuilding pays, but not so tangled that characterization tests are impossible?
Does the asset purchase agreement transfer IP, domains, accounts and customer contracts cleanly?
Would a treasury bill beat this deal's downside case over the payback period?
Did the earned-autonomy loop check stop_reason, or could refusals have passed as success?
validation_oracles: Read-only processor exports and bank statements reconciled to the listing within 5%.
A lawyer's review of the asset purchase agreement and the compliance gap list; an escrow service holding funds until transfer.
The characterization test suite passing on the old app before the rewrite and on the new app after each strangler step.
Post-close monthly churn from the processor versus the pre-close cohort baseline, with the 10% falsifier threshold.
Actual rebuild hours logged in predictions.json scored against the paper estimate.
failure_modes: Screenshot revenue: seller dashboards overstate. Tell: numbers do not reconcile to deposits. Fix: require processor read-only access and bank statements before shortlisting.

Rank, not code: traffic from one search ranking collapses after migration changes URLs. Tell: Search Console shows most revenue from a few pages. Fix: preserve URLs and redirects; treat SEO as a core flow.
Rewrite before understanding: agents rewrite flows nobody tested. Tell: support tickets spike after cutover. Fix: characterization tests first, strangler migration one flow at a time.
Inherited liability: public buckets or undeleted uploads exist at close. Tell: compliance table rows marked present. Fix: fix before migration and negotiate escrow holdback.
Silent agent failures: refusals returned as HTTP 200 counted as success. Tell: tasks pass but output is empty or a refusal text. Fix: check stop_reason and revoke autonomy below 90% pass rate.
Estimate optimism: hours ignore migration and support. Tell: actual hours exceed the high estimate in month one. Fix: re-underwrite with actuals and stop if payback breaks.
agent_direction: Start with Acquire.com and Flippa listing data, then stop and hand the shortlist and request lists to the user, because data room access, NDAs and seller contact are the user's actions. Cache listings and every tool output under a deals/ folder per listing. Once repo access exists, spawn one sub-agent per shortlisted repo for step 2 tool runs in isolated worktrees, and review their findings by spot-checking three tool outputs each. Run steps 3 to 5 yourself, since they are judgment-heavy. Never paste secrets found by gitleaks into any report. Never run reverse-engineering tools on apps the user does not own or have written permission to analyze. Stop and ask when revenue cannot be verified, when a legal question decides the verdict, or before any communication with a seller. Return final_report.md as the entry point, with listings.parquet, tech_dd.md files, rebuild_spec.md, compliance_perf_gaps.md, underwriting.csv, predictions.json and post_close_plan.md beside it.

mission: Produces a scan-to-parametric-CAD pipeline in which a coding agent takes a mesh of a real object (from the Orbiter smartphone rig, photogrammetry, or a Raspberry Pi LiDAR handheld), fits geometric primitives to the contact surfaces, writes a CadQuery script for a mount with a stated clearance, slices it through a CLI the agent builds itself, and logs iterations-to-fit against the maker's own hand CAD on three objects. Done means three printed parts with caliper-verified fit, a measured scan error budget, and a falsifier verdict on whether agent CAD needs fewer print iterations than hand CAD.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A mechanical design engineer would start with an error budget, not a scan: scanner accuracy, mesh-to-primitive fitting error, printer dimensional error, and the clearance they want, each measured. They would print a clearance test coupon first (holes and pegs at 0.1 to 0.5 mm steps) so the agent's '0.3 mm clearance' means something on this printer and filament. ROLE AND STANCE
You are a mechanical design engineer and automation developer. Goal: prove or disprove that an agent can turn a scan of a real object into a parametric part that fits on the first or second print. Source claims to test: Orbiter promises 'a perfect fit on the first try' from a smartphone scan; Peppa Cam says a Pi LiDAR handheld is fine 'for most scanning jobs'; a Claude-to-Blender demo built a whole scene as Python; the 'build yourself a CLI tool' pattern lets an agent control any program without an MCP; text-to-CAD sites claim complete CAD models from a sentence.

CONTEXT
- Scanners: Orbiter (smartphone rig), photogrammetry via COLMAP or Meshroom, Peppa Cam Raspberry Pi LiDAR, LingBot-Map video-to-3D.
- Geometry: Open3D, trimesh, pyransac3d, CloudCompare.
- CAD: CadQuery or build123d (Python), FreeCAD fallback, Blender Python only for visualization.
- Slicing: PrusaSlicer or OrcaSlicer CLI.
- Hardware: the user's FDM printer, calipers, a ChArUco board printed at known scale.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
1. Every dimension in the CAD is a named parameter traceable to a fitted primitive or a caliper reading.
2. The scan is not trusted until three caliper checks per object agree within 0.3 mm.
3. Clearance is chosen from a printed coupon on this printer and filament, not assumed.
4. Write the go/no-go fit criterion per object before printing it.
5. The hand-CAD control is done by the user without seeing the agent's CAD.

DELIVERABLES IN ORDER
1. coupon.py (CadQuery), coupon.stl and the recommended clearance after the user's measurements.
2. capture_protocol.md for each object and scanner.
3. fit_primitives.py: clean mesh, segment marked contact regions, fit planes and cylinders, report residual RMS and the fitted parameters as JSON.
4. scan_check.md: caliper vs scan for three features per object; CloudCompare deviation vs a reference object.
5. One CadQuery script per object with STEP and STL output and a parameter table.
6. slicecli: an agent-built command-line wrapper around PrusaSlicer with orientation, profile and support flags, returning G-code path, time and grams.
7. fit_log.csv: object, method (agent or hand), iteration, parameters changed, caliper readings, fit verdict.
8. report.md with iterations-to-fit per object and method and the falsifier verdict.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
Before finishing, list in GAPS: surfaces where primitive fitting failed (organic shapes like a tool handle grip); scale uncertainty; printer drift between iterations; any object where the hand CAD and agent CAD used different clearances; claims you could not test (for example LingBot-Map accuracy if not run). Fill gaps you can, such as re-fitting with a different primitive or adding a freeform offset surface from the mesh, and record the result.

SELF-QUESTIONS
- Which surfaces actually bear the load or locate the part, and did I fit only those?
- Is the scan scaled from a known reference, or is photogrammetry scale arbitrary?
- Is my clearance compensating for printer error that a slicer setting (horizontal expansion, elephant-foot compensation) should fix instead?
- Does print orientation change the fit dimension more than my clearance?
- For organic shapes, should the part be a mesh offset instead of primitives?

STOP CONDITIONS
Stop and report if scan error exceeds 0.3 mm after two capture attempts, or if after three iterations an object still fails fit; record which error source dominated.

RETURN FORMAT
A table of iterations-to-fit by object and method, falsifier verdict, file list, GAPS, and self-question answers.

validation_oracles: The physical fit on each real object, judged against a go/no-go criterion written before printing.
Caliper measurements of printed contact features versus CadQuery parameters, within the coupon-derived tolerance.
CloudCompare deviation of scans versus a calibration cube or gauge block of known size.
The user's blind hand-CAD iteration counts on the same three objects, as the control.

failure_modes: Unscaled scan: photogrammetry mesh is uniformly 2% off. Tell: every printed dimension misses by the same ratio. Fix: scale from the ChArUco board or a reference cube in frame.
Fitting the wrong surface: agent fits a cosmetic face instead of the locating one. Tell: part sits but rocks or slides. Fix: user marks contact regions explicitly; fit only those.

Clearance fighting printer bias: holes print undersized and clearance is raised every iteration. Tell: iterations change the same parameter in the same direction. Fix: apply slicer XY hole compensation from the coupon, reset clearance.
Organic shapes forced into primitives: grip fit fails with high residual. Tell: RMS above 0.2 mm on that region. Fix: mesh offset subtraction for organic regions.
Orientation distortion: critical bore printed vertically becomes oval. Tell: caliper shows different diameters across axes. Fix: reorient in slicecli or split the part.
Silent slicer defaults: CLI ignores a misspelled profile name. Tell: print time differs from expected. Fix: slicecli validates profile names and exits non-zero.

ROLE AND STANCE
You are a learning scientist and agent engineer. You will run the benchmark-gated skill-optimization loop on a person instead of a prompt. Source claims to test: SkillOpt rejects any skill edit that does not beat the benchmark and beats hand-written prompts; a bilevel outer 'coach' loop is about 5x better on Karpathy's autoresearch benchmark; skills that log their own failures and get batch-rewritten improve; turning saves into quizzes beats passive watching; mining chat history yields better instructions. Treat each as a hypothesis.

CONTEXT
- Study set: the user's saves from the last 60 days; DejaViewed parquet has titles, captions, transcripts, takeaways.
- Eval set: held-out retrieval questions generated from source transcripts.
- Control: FSRS spaced-repetition flashcards (py-fsrs or Anki).
- Optional input: exported Claude or ChatGPT history (conversations.json).
- Budget: about 20 minutes per topic per week of honest self-quizzing.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
1. Item bank frozen before week 1; record its SHA-256. No question is edited after the user sees it.
2. Questions are generated in a context that sees only source material, never study notes, playbooks or prior answers.
3. The coach changes at most one playbook element per week and the change is kept only if the next held-out score on coach topics beats the incumbent.
4. The control topic gets equal minutes and no coach.
5. Quizzes are taken cold: no notes, no search, no AI. Scores are self-reported; the agent must not invent them.
6. Chat-history mining stays local; redact names, emails and credentials before any analysis.

1. topics.json: clusters, chosen topics, difficulty proxy, random assignment with seed.

3. playbook_v1.md and coach skill (prompt plus rules) with the accept-only-if-better gate.
4. session_log.parquet and issues.parquet schemas, plus the weekly script that samples 5 items per topic, collects scores, and runs the coach.
5. chat_mining.py: local pass that finds questions the user asked more than once.
6. analysis.md at week 6 plus 14 days: learning curves, coach minus control with bootstrap intervals, minimum detectable effect, blind delayed-test results, never-stuck topics, falsifier verdict.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
Write GAPS: weeks with missed quizzes; any item that leaked into study material; topics whose difficulty was mismatched; items the second grader scored differently by more than one point; claims you could not test. SELF-QUESTIONS
- Are the coach and control topics comparable in difficulty and prior knowledge, and how do I know?
- With 15 items and 5 sampled per week, what is the smallest improvement I could detect?
- Could held-out items have leaked through study notes the generator produced?
- Is a week-over-week rise just practice on repeated items rather than learning?
- Did the coach's accepted edits improve the delayed test, or only the next-week quiz?

STOP CONDITIONS

RETURN FORMAT
Falsifier verdict, learning curve table per topic, coach minus control with interval, never-stuck topics, the file list, GAPS, and self-question answers.

gap_audit_prompt: You are an independent reviewer of a six-week benchmark-your-brain experiment. List missing pieces: missed weeks, topics with too few items, external tasks not run. self_questions: Are coach and control topics matched in difficulty and prior knowledge, or did I pick an easy control?
Could any held-out question have appeared in study notes or a generated summary?
With 15 items per topic, is the effect I hope for even detectable?

Are my self-grades systematically kinder than the blind grader's?
Which saves were too thin to support real questions, and did they bias topic choice?
Did chat-history mining surface re-asked questions I actually need, and were they kept out of the eval bank?

validation_oracles: A delayed test 14 days after the last session, graded by a second grader blind to condition.
The flashcard control topic on FSRS with matched minutes, as the comparison arm.
bank_hash.txt matching the item bank at every weekly check, proving the eval was frozen.
External tasks where available: Database Detective or SQLBolt exercises for SQL topics, a working build for coding topics.

failure_modes: Eval leakage: question generator saw the study notes, so quizzes test memorized notes. Tell: near-perfect scores in week 1. Fix: regenerate from sources only and replace leaked items from reserve.
Noise-chasing coach: accepts edits on one-item differences. Tell: playbook flips back and forth weekly. Fix: require a margin at least the week-to-week standard deviation before accepting.
Unmatched control: the control topic is easier or already known. Tell: control prior-knowledge rating differs by 2 or more. Fix: redraw with seed before week 1.
Repetition masquerading as learning: same items each week. Tell: scores rise on repeated items only. Fix: follow the sampling plan and analyze first-exposure items separately.
Self-grading drift: rubric applied more kindly over time. Tell: blind grader disagreement rises across weeks. Fix: use blind grades for all conclusions.
Dropout: missed weeks break the loop. Tell: gaps in session_log. Fix: schedule quizzes as a recurring routine and pause the coach on missed weeks.
